chunks: What is etching?. The question: What is etching?
Etching removes material from the wafer in a chosen pattern.
After lithography (printing with light) leaves a stencil of resist, etching eats away the thin layer (film) in the openings, so the pattern becomes part of the chip itself.
Wet etching uses a liquid chemical. Dry etching uses a plasma, which is an electrically charged gas. Modern chips need dry etching because it cuts straight down.
Picture sandblasting through a stencil. The sand flies straight down, so the cut matches the stencil's openings with straight walls. That is dry etching.
Now picture dipping the same stencil in a bath of acid. The liquid also creeps sideways under the stencil's edges. That is wet etching.
That creep is harmless for big shapes but ruins tiny lines.
In the film layer (blue outline), the isotropic etch (left) removes material under the resist as well, so the opening is wider than the pattern by about the depth on each side.
The anisotropic plasma etch (right) keeps the walls vertical, so the feature width matches the resist opening.
Mask: the protective layer, such as resist, that covers areas you want to keep. Isotropic: etching equally in all directions, so it eats sideways as fast as down.
Anisotropic: etching mainly in one direction, usually straight down. Undercut: sideways etching beneath the edge of the mask.
Selectivity: how many times faster the etch removes the target film than the mask or layers beneath.
Plasma: a gas energized so it contains charged particles and reactive fragments.
Say you etch a 100 nm film isotropically under a mask line 1 µm (1000 nm) wide. The undercut is about 100 nm on each side, so the line shrinks to 1000 minus 200 = 800 nm.
A 50 nm line would vanish. A directional plasma etch keeps the width near its drawn size. Selectivity sets how thick the mask must be.
To etch 500 nm of oxide (glass) with a 5:1 selectivity to the resist, plus 20% extra etch time to clear leftovers, you need at least 1. 2 times 500 ÷ 5 = 120 nm of resist.
That is the whole idea.
"Etching selectively removes material to transfer the resist pattern into the actual film.
Wet etching uses liquid chemicals: cheap and selective but mostly isotropic, so it undercuts.
Dry or plasma etching, reactive-ion etching, uses reactive gas plus ion bombardment to cut vertical sidewalls, which is what fine features need.
The key specs are etch rate, anisotropy and selectivity to the mask and underlying layer."
